title: Estimating spacetime fluctuation strength in SU(1,1) and SU(2) interferometers
abstract: High-precision laser interferometers are commonly used to search for signatures of random spacetime fluctuations, in an attempt to understand the fundamental nature of gravity. Conventionally, $SU(2)$ interferometers have been used in such experimental investigations. Motivated by [K. Zheng \textit{et al.}, Photon. Res. \textbf{8}, 1653 (2020)], I assess if there is any advantage to be gained by using an $SU(1,1)$ interferometer instead of the $SU(2)$ interferometer. To this end, I compute the quantum Fisher information for estimating the strength and the correlation length of the spacetime fluctuations, and the corresponding classical Fisher information considering different experimentally relevant measurement schemes, in both types of interferometers. I compare the information metrics corresponding to different parameter regimes that are relevant to both current and possible future experimental setups. This helps me assess if and when the $SU(1,1)$ interferometer offers any advantage over the $SU(2)$ interferometer for estimating either the fluctuation strength or correlation length of the spacetime fluctuations.
summary: This paper theoretically compares two types of laser interferometers, SU(2) and SU(1,1), for detecting subtle signatures of random spacetime fluctuations. By calculating Fisher information metrics, the authors assess when the alternative SU(1,1) geometry provides a superior measurement sensitivity compared to the standard SU(2) setup. The findings suggest that while theoretically promising, realizing this advantage requires significant technological advancements beyond current experimental capabilities.
main_problem: The study aims to determine if using an SU(1,1) interferometer offers a measurable advantage over the conventional SU(2) interferometer for estimating spacetime fluctuation strength and correlation length.
main_result: For current experimental parameters, the SU(1,1) setup shows no advantage; however, theoretical analysis suggests it could outperform SU(2) under future conditions involving significant technological improvements.
method: The authors compute both Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) and classical Fisher information (CFI) metrics for Gaussian input states in both interferometer types.
model_or_system: The physical system is a high-precision laser interferometer, modeled using SU(2) and SU(1,1) transformations. The analysis incorporates the effects of internal losses ($\eta$) on the quantum state evolution.
key_observables: Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) and classical Fisher information metrics for estimating fluctuation strength ($\Gamma$) and correlation length ($\ell$).
important_parameters: Spacetime fluctuation strength ($\Gamma$), correlation length ($\ell$), internal loss ($\eta$), squeezing parameter ($ eta$), and input coherent state amplitude ($\alpha$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the long wavelength limit, uses Gaussian states, and compares performance under both lossless and lossy conditions.
figures_summary: Figures compare scaled QFI and CFIs for SU(2) vs. SU(1,1) across different squeezing regimes; Table I summarizes ratios of Fisher information metrics.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem by comparing SU(2) and SU(1,1). It details the calculation of QFI and CFI using quadrature operators for Gaussian states. The core is a comparative analysis showing performance under current vs. future technological regimes to assess potential advantages.
why_interesting: This work applies advanced quantum metrology techniques (QFI/CFI) to fundamental physics problems in general relativity, specifically testing the limits of spacetime measurement using quantum optics.
